findings.claim: `reboots_sent` is incremented for every row in `attempts`, including reservations with no recorded outcome. The service durably inserts that reservation before calling `client.reboot()`, so a crash in between can leave an attempt counted as a reboot sent when no command was issued. This makes the report's documented “reboots sent” metric overstate known sends.
findings.title: The report counts reserved attempts as reboots sent

findings.claim: The report selects `durations[len(durations) // 2]` as `outage_median_s`. For an even number of measured outages this returns only the upper middle duration rather than the median (the average of the two middle values), so the documented median is inaccurate for those samples.
findings.title: Even-sized outage samples report the upper middle value, not the median

findings.claim: The new preflight-failure handling durably auth-latches on `UNSUPPORTED`. But the preflight calls `GetDeviceInformation`, while the unsupported-reboot claim concerns `SystemReboot`; a camera rejecting the read operation can therefore be blocked from recovery until operator acknowledgement even though reboot support was never tested. The fault classifier maps generic unsupported-operation faults to `UNSUPPORTED`.
findings.title: Unsupported preflight operation can latch recovery as if reboot were unsupported

findings.claim: The report increments `reboots_sent` for every row in `attempts`, but dispatch records that row during reservation before calling `client.reboot()`. A process interruption after reservation and before the send therefore appears in the report as a reboot sent, contrary to the report's documented meaning.
findings.title: Report can overstate reserved attempts as reboots sent

findings.claim: `reboots_sent` is incremented for every row in `attempts`, but attempts are durably inserted before `client.reboot()` is called. If the process stops in between, the report still counts a reboot as sent even though no ONVIF request was issued, making the effectiveness report inaccurate.
findings.title: Report counts reserved attempts as reboots sent

findings.claim: The new README calls development-plan.md a “Reviewed development plan,” but that plan explicitly marks both its amendment self-audit and independent re-review as pending. This misstates the approval status of the active plan to readers relying on the project contract links.
findings.title: README labels the development plan reviewed while its amendment review is pending

findings.claim: The README says the current tests/unit regression suite passes 48 tests and 32 subtests, while the milestone ledger reports the same `tests/unit -q` command passing 66 tests and 65 subtests. These conflicting current-result claims make the documented qualification evidence unreliable.
findings.title: README and milestone ledger report conflicting test-suite totals

findings.claim: The catalogue’s `productIDs` trims surrounding whitespace before those IDs are requested from StoreKit, but the joiner looks up products using the original, untrimmed catalogue values. For an ID with surrounding whitespace, StoreKit can return the requested product while the join fails to associate it with its plan, so that cadence is absent from the subscription list.
findings.title: Normalized product IDs are joined using their unnormalized values

findings.claim: Catalogue `productIDs` trims surrounding whitespace before requesting StoreKit products, but the joiner looks up StoreKit results using the untrimmed monthly/yearly catalogue values. If a configured ID has surrounding whitespace, StoreKit can return the trimmed ID while the joiner drops that cadence, leaving the plan unavailable despite a successful product request.
findings.title: Trimmed catalogue product IDs fail to join StoreKit results

findings.claim: HAProxy forwards epcore requests with Host and SNI epcore.effectivepolicy.com.au to 172.31.1.60:9443. Thus this route has no matching epcore vhost in the change and may serve a default vhost or fail instead of the intended application.
findings.title: Epcore backend has no matching vhost among the added event-Apache configs

findings.claim: The epcore backend sends traffic to 172.31.1.60:9443, but the added Effective Policy FPM vhost binds only to 127.0.0.1:8083 and names effectivepolicy.com.au/www.effectivepolicy.com.au. That vhost cannot receive the edge-routed epcore request, leaving it to fail or reach another listener/vhost.
findings.title: Epcore edge route does not match the added FPM vhost

findings.claim: The LMS backend connects to 172.31.1.60:443, while the added lms-dev Apache vhost listens on 172.31.1.60:9443. Consequently, requests routed by this backend will not reach the new vhost or its dedicated PHP-FPM handler.

findings.claim: The tier mapper assigns `.nativeStorage` to any primitive-target test whose function name contains `sqlite` or `sigkill`, and `requiredEvidence` makes the STORE-07 and STORE-09 SQLite tests certifying variants. Those tests instantiate `SQLiteProbeStore`, explicitly described as test-local and not product code; the `SessionStore` interface also says SQL lives in M2-A. Consequently, passing this coverage gate can mark STORE-07/09 satisfied even if the eventual production store violates their contracts.
findings.title: Test-local SQLite probe is counted as native-storage certification

findings.claim: BASE stores /data in ./data, while HEAD mounts the separate watchdog_data volume. An existing deployment that follows the new setup without copying its state.db will use a fresh store: the service initializes a database when the file is absent, while safety records and recovery limits are persisted there. This can make prior attempt budgets, cooldowns, or latches invisible and allow recovery actions that the old store would have blocked. Document or provide a migration path before switching the canonical volume.
findings.title: Compose volume change can bypass persisted recovery limits on upgrade

findings.claim: The report sorts measured outage durations but selects `durations[len(durations) // 2]`. findings.claim: The LMS dev HAProxy backend connects to 172.31.1.60:443, while the added LMS dev vhost listens on 172.31.1.60:9443 and uses the new LMS PHP-FPM socket. Consequently, requests routed through this backend cannot reach that vhost or pool; if this backend is meant to activate the added FPM configuration, LMS dev continues to use a different listener. The behavior of any existing :443 vhost is not established here.
findings.title: LMS dev backend bypasses its new event-Apache vhost

findings.claim: The admin and cart rate limits only track and reject requests when CF-Connecting-IP is present, and use its value as the tracking key. The new backend rules also pass that header through as X-Real-IP (lines 234–282). If a direct non-Cloudflare request can reach the edge, a caller can omit the header to skip these limits or supply changing values to evade per-IP tracking, while spoofing the IP reported to backends. The existing live HAProxy configuration instead sets X-Real-IP from the connection source. A network-level Cloudflare-only ingress restriction could mitigate this, but none is established in the reviewed configuration.
findings.title: Client-supplied Cloudflare IP header can bypass rate limits

findings.claim: The BASE edge configuration sent epcore to 172.31.1.60:443; HEAD sends it to 172.31.1.60:9443 with Host epcore.effectivepolicy.com.au. The added Effective Policy FPM vhost is loopback-only on 127.0.0.1:8083 and declares effectivepolicy.com.au/www, while the added :9443 vhosts declare other hosts. Thus the new epcore route has no matching epcore vhost in the added event-Apache configuration and may serve the wrong site or fail.
findings.title: Epcore routes to :9443 without a matching vhost

findings.claim: BASE's public Codable CaseResult encoded without evidence_tier; HEAD adds a non-optional EvidenceLayer and coding key but no backward-compatible decoding default. Synthesized decoding therefore rejects prior result JSON that omits the field. This is a compatibility regression for downstream consumers that persist or exchange CaseResult payloads; no such decoder is visible in-tree, so the impact is conditional.
findings.title: New required evidence_tier breaks decoding of existing CaseResult JSON

findings.claim: BASE exposed CaseResult as Codable without an evidence_tier field; HEAD adds a non-optional EvidenceLayer and its evidence_tier coding key. With synthesized Codable, an existing serialized record lacking that key cannot be decoded, despite the initializer’s .pure default. This can break consumers of previously emitted reports; no migration or versioning is visible here. Whether persisted reports are in use is uncertain.
findings.title: Adding evidence_tier breaks decoding of existing CaseResult JSON

findings.claim: BASE's public Codable CaseResult had no evidence_tier field, so JSON it encoded lacks that key. HEAD adds evidenceTier as a non-optional property and maps it to evidence_tier; synthesized decoding therefore requires the new key, so consumers that persist or exchange BASE-format results will fail to decode them. The initializer's .pure default does not supply a decoding default. No in-repository persisted-result decoder was found, so impact on downstream consumers is uncertain.
findings.title: Adding evidence_tier makes prior CaseResult JSON undecodable

findings.claim: The backend receives X-Real-IP from the request's CF-Connecting-IP header, and the edge also keys its login rate limit on that header. If non-Cloudflare clients can reach the public edge listener, they can forge or rotate this header to spoof the backend client IP and evade the per-IP rate limit. BASE instead set the backend X-Real-IP from the socket source. External network restrictions may mitigate this, but none are established in the inspected repository evidence.
findings.title: Client-supplied Cloudflare IP header controls backend identity and rate limits

findings.claim: The ingestion gate requires the SQLite contract tests to certify STORE-07 and STORE-09, but those tests execute `SQLiteProbeStore`, explicitly marked as test-local and not product code. The catalogue defines these as native-storage requirements, while the `SessionStore` source says SQL belongs to M2-A. Thus a broken or absent production storage implementation would not prevent these probe tests from passing and the coverage gate from marking those cases satisfied.
findings.title: Test-local SQLite probe certifies product storage cases

findings.claim: This required-evidence mapping makes STORE_02_sigkillMidTransactionRollsBack a certifying variant, and the ingestion test requires every mapped case to appear satisfied. But that probe only commits a generic row, kills a separate sqlite3 process during an uncommitted insert, and verifies rollback; it does not exercise crashes before/after an intent or side effect, or prevent automatic side-effect replay as STORE-02 requires. The M2-0 coverage run can therefore report STORE-02 satisfied while the production-store crash qualification remains outstanding.
findings.title: STORE-02 is certified by a generic SQLite rollback probe
